Ok so I've been playing for a long time now and I cant in good conscious just openly recommend PGR but I will say it is if your willing to stick with it, it is easily one of the most rewarding games you could ever play in just watching its constant improvement over the years until it essentially just become peak. The story has a very rough start and has some pacing issues towards the beginning and middle of what's available it has constantly improved and by the time your halfway through what is currently available its incredibly satisfying to read and for the many MANY hours to days of reading it could take i would not have traded this story for anything. Gameplay is fairly fun with its best works always being boss fights, characters all have pretty unique playstyles especially for the limitations of controls that come from the fact that this game is playable on mobile though i wouldn't recommend it, And they continue to make characters that keep iterating and adding upon what exists. Lastly is the gacha aspect which is a pain point for many people the only thing i can say is its definitely one of the more generous games with frequent opportunities to get rerun characters and often Kuro just decides to just give out a selector for free sometimes cause why not. Characters get powercrept but never truly leave viability like many other gacha in the space, and the game focuses primarily on adding new forms to older characters allowing favorite characters to never really become truly gone from the story which is nice. Honestly makes me feel like a One Piece fan recommending the game but honestly atleast give it a try, its free.

[h1]Welcome eveyone, to the greatest game you've never heard of.[/h1] I have been playing this game since the global release back in July 2021, and the gameplay still amazes me to this day. Made by the same dev of Wuthering Waves.....PGR is brutal, fast and stylish. Its a hack n' slash action rpg that takes heavy inspiration from Nier: Automata (which they collab'd with) that adds a unique "ping orb" system inplace of regular skills. Boss fights are extremely thought out (the later ones at least) and even have their own special parry animations with certain characters. [h3]SOUNDTRACK[/h3] Easily the only reason why im making a lengthy review on this game. I found out about this game not from the gameplay, but the music. Vanguard Sound Studio creates the most epic, ethereal, emotional and absolute BANGER tracks you'd never expect from a game like this. Certain tracks are actually synced to certain boss fight moves which makes them even more memorable. Here are some tracks to get you started: Narwhal, Dust, Hikari, Moonlit Occultation, To The Limit, In My Memory, Exorcism, Under Dimension, Crossing Eternities [h3]THE ELEPHANT[/h3] Im addressing this ahead of time.........yes, this is a GACHA GAME. However, its possibly the most generous gacha games of this era. If you complete all the weeklies and events for the patch, you will have enough to pity the next character in the next patch. Despite that, you dont really have to pull on the gacha unless you like to be high on the leaderboard for the competitive modes (warzone, Pain cage). All story content has a forced story character to use and the events has a trial character you can use to clear said event. Everyone talks about meta and must pull teams but.......it doesnt matter. You can clear the game just fine with whatever you want to do. [h3]CHARACTERS[/h3] All characters are extremely well designed....from their unique animations to small details, and the abilities they have. Some can parry, block, reversal, execution, counter, change forms, go into burst mode, etc.... Also dont get caught on A-ranks being useless. Most of them are more fun to play than most of the recently released S-ranks and can clear content just as fine. All you gotta do is just dodge [h3]THE STORY[/h3] Luckily they recently improved the new player experience by making the story less confusing. Now every story chapter is in a timeline structure so there is no confusion on "whats next" and the boring early chapters condensed into only the important parts so you can get to the good (yet depressing) chapters. The story also includes perspectives on the political sides of war, which is a unique touch i rarely see. [h3]PRO TIPS[/h3] - For my ultrawide users, Alt+Enter will make the game fullscreen. dont worry about the ingame resolution settings. - The game does support controller, dont let Steam mislead you. There is a toggle for Controller mode in the Button Position setting. Also i had to disable steams' controller mode thing as it was interfering with my binds. - Never pull on Fate banner. not even for whales. - There are plenty of ways to get free s-rank characters. Dorm commission shop, vouchers, Thunderbolt Manual, service shop and many selectors from logins and new player missions. - Pain Cage is your main source to upgrade your s-ranks to SS. voucher shop helps too - Under the Study tab in the Battle screen, there is Celica's Class which you can try out different boss fights at any time. they also give out Black Cards on first clear.

This really doesn’t feel right on PC. The whole thing still feels like a mobile port — the UI, the menus, the controls — everything clearly comes from a phone. It never feels properly adapted for keyboard and mouse, and that gets annoying very fast. Using a controller helps, a lot. With a PS or Xbox controller it’s way more playable and the combat feels smoother. But even then, the interface is still very mobile-focused, so it never fully clicks as a PC game. The combat itself is fun and flashy, so the game isn’t bad at its core. The problem is the platform. On PC it feels awkward, clunky, and out of place. If you really want to try it, use a controller. But honestly, I wouldn’t recommend playing this on PC.

I've been playing PGR ever since the Grand Blue patch in 2022. When I first started playing I instantly fell in love with it. It used to tick all my boxes: great combat, amazing music, beautiful designs with a varied cast of characters, generous gacha, but most importantly it required actual skill to play. The story was so-so, but when I reached Chapter 12 I realized that I was invested without even realizing, and the best part was yet to come. And it did. But this review is about the game nowadays. My thoughts as someone who's logged in every single day for 4+ years now. Let's start from what PGR is most known for: [h2]1) The Combat[/h2] Years ago, PGR was known as "the most skill-based gacha game in the market", and it actually used to be true. The enemies and bosses were ruthless, you had little to no i-frames to abuse, positioning mattered and on top of that you had to manage your orbs. While the weekly modes weren't (still aren't) anything to write home about, the true spotlight at the time was Babel Tower, a game mode with stage and enemy gimmicks that were HARD. Positioning mattered, stamina management mattered or else you were dead. Over the course of the years the gameplay shifted significantly. What was once a struggle for survival nowadays is a walk in the park. The philosophy shifted from skill requirement to accessibility via simplified orb gameplay, i-frame spam, ult spam, timestop... ultimately it led to characters being designed less for fun and more for performing well in the 2 weekly modes we've had since launch. Babel Tower is a JOKE, it doesn't even have stage or enemy gimmicks anymore. We've had some experiments like Trial of Simulacrum which focuses on stylish play and Rapid Pursuit, but they jut highlight how boring and samey characters feel nowadays, their movesets lack dynamic gameplay and are too linear. In the end it makes sense why they did this: gacha players always focus more on weekly endgame modes, which don't mesh with the previous gameplay philosophy. Was there a better solution? Maybe, but it's too late now. Characters deal truckloads of damage all over the stage while the enemies are frozen in time and don't have time to act before you've already ulted again. As a result, enemy and boss designs took a hit, they aren't engaging as much and their mechanics aren't as fleshed out as they used to be. It's not a "you control the buttons you press" case, this is core design problems. It ain't the same anymore. TBF there are exceptions from time to time. A-rank units offer some interesting gameplay mechanics, but due to their lack of damage and timestop they aren't viable in the meta. Rosetta: Arete, who's the newest S-rank frame at the time of this review, I actually think is one of the best characters they've ever made, as she uses an orb system that allows her to pop different moves at all times, have her switch forms seamlessly and actual airborne combat, the same systems used with the Sparda bros for the DMC5 collab. Only time will tell if they're going to keep this up or if they'll fall back down into the trap they've been stuck in for years. But enemy design is still a problem. Balancing is also a mess nowadays, Veronica and Rosetta being the most egregious examples of Kuro not knowing wtf they're up to. The former ended up borderline useless and the latter is so broken that she powercreeps a barely 4-month old unit if you haven't spent lots of resources on her. They're exceptions rather than the standard, but recently they've been making balancing decisions only possible by being high on crack. [h2]2) The Characters[/h2] PGR sports a varied cast of both male and female characters, taking into account the gacha antics of the girls being more than the dudes. You have the Gray Raven trio of Lucia, Liv and Lee + other squads and factions. Most the cast is very well written (personal standouts being Vera and Noan), some are just alright or outright forgotten like Sophia and Changyu. Instead of releasing a new character every patch, PGR focuses mostly on its already established cast by giving them new frames. There are also some NPCs that could always turn out to be playable in the future, recent examples of this being Discord and Veronica. Coolest thing about PGR's designs is that everyone's an android, so they aren't afraid to show off mechanical bodies with a militaristic vibe to match. Ball joints, translucent body parts, functional armament... it's a big part of PGR's appeal. Back then the game was on the less fanservicey side, the designs weren't revealing at all and most of the fanservice was in affection stories, limited time events and skins. Also helped that the game used to not shy away from releasing both male and female units pretty consistently and the rest of the game took itself pretty seriously. But with the passage of time the gender ratio got nuked, the designs got bolder and less mechanical/militaristic and other stuff that I'll touch upon in the story section of the review. The feedback on this shift wasn't positive in neither the global and Asian side of things, with people worrying if PGR was losing its visual identity and Kuro themselves asking their opinions on this via surveys, so for the next lineup they revealed returning characters with fully mechanical bodies, starting from the current Rosetta: Arete [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lPy5kGusljI](of which they even made a showcase of every single detail and functionality built into her)[/url], Kamui who was kept waiting since launch and was thus highly demanded and Alpha, who's THE fan-favorite all around and the most famous PGR character. Maybe they're going back to what made PGR stand out, only one way to find out. [h2]3) The Story[/h2] Ask someone their opinion on the story and they'll say it's good, because it is! Some chapters I feel don't belong in a gacha game. But ever since Chapter 31's success they've been failing miserably to replicate what made it good, and the current arc has sucked for the most part. Most of the budget goes into affection and coating stories rather than the main story which is sad. It's hard to talk about it without spoiling, the most I'll say is that they've been trying to shoehorn romance a lot more without any real buildup like in ch31's case. Even the Babylonia mode is made mostly for dating characters rather than as a storytelling method (though with the newest main story chapter they finally made use of it for its prologue, so maybe it's going to be a standard from now on) [h1]Why is this review negative?[/h1] TLDR: i find modern PGR to be a shell of its former self. A game that's way past its prime. It fluctuates between high quality and unpolished trash, and for a new player it's hard to get into because of the sheer amount of stuff and terrible newbie experience. If my overall problems with the game don't seem like they'll bother you then you'll have a lot of fun, as for me, there's still a lot of things I value that keep me attached to it. I love the story, its characters, the music... but I used to love it more, and it's not just burnout talking - there's a spark that's lacking nowadays, and I hope Kuro will be able to put it back in a bottle. They're on the right track overall, but it can easily slip away. Only one way to find out. I'll leave the comments open, feel free to ask any questions to stuff I can't fit into the review's character limit.

Combat is great. The VFX, SFX, and character designs are all top notch along with some great music. The roguelikes are some of my favorite in the genre, in particular Cursed Waves. The Godfall Revelation was very fun. Story and lore are pretty interesting as well. However, my issues with the game are always front and center when I log in. My least enjoyable modes happen to be the weekly modes being Warzone and Pain Cage, which are 2 of the endgame modes that hold the vast majority of pulls and character upgrade mats. Running these at lower difficulties substantially decreases upgrade mats, and the recent additions to the rewards in Pain Cage only apply to the higher difficulty. I attempted adjusting how I play to only do what I enjoy, but the game is not designed to accommodate that playstyle if you want to continue getting characters and building them. Aside from my standard issues with the gacha genre of power creep, uninteresting events, shallow minigames/side activities, etc, PGR failed me by its reward structure and lack of choice in gameplay difficulty. It's a shame. If there were a game in the genre that could win me over, this was probably it. Why not play the higher difficulty? Rank determines the rewards you get. Higher difficulty = competing with high spenders = lower rank for low spenders = lower rewards, add the fact that you are now required to pull to keep your current ranking. Essentially, a hamster wheel. You pull to retain your current rank/rewards. If you hop off the hamster wheel at any point, you lose rewards. Don't like a character? Too bad. They're much more powerful than your current roster and those you're competing with are using them. Hope you enjoy getting pennies and not being able to build the majority of your roster when your peers are getting significantly more. I tried to get out of this cycle by, as stated above, only playing the modes I'm having fun with, but since the majority of rewards are in endgame, I found that there's just too little to do for not much in return.

Don't let my playtime on Steam fool ya, I have actually played PGR all the way back in September of 2021 on Bluestacks before a PC client was even thought of. I did take a long break and came back on Alpha's Crimson Weave patch though. Loved this game a lot, but that ultimately is no longer the case anymore and I would never recommend it anymore unless Kuro fixes their downward spiral into greed and ignorance. Also, this review was made during Alpha's Inverse Crown patch, ironic how I came back on an Alpha patch and then inevitably lose my love on an Alpha patch. who is in fact my favorite character; woah so generic. Back in the day, PGR was one of the most F2P-friendly gacha games out there. Generally providing enough Black Cards during each patch with some free or A-Rank patches that function as a saving patch. That is technically still the case, but the last free patch was Nirvatia's Dirge at the time of this review, Kamui Aeternion wasn't free or A-Rank and Alpha Inverse Crown isn't free and is actually limited like Liv Limpidity was. The Phylotree has been the most obvious trend of PGR degrading from its former glory, Kuro never used FOMO at all and all Constructs released would be put in the general pool. That is not the case anymore with Limited Phylotree Constructs, they are only available on their Patch and a potential rerun; which Liv Limpidity was in fact reran except... On Alpha Inverse Crown's patch, so if ya missed Liv Limpidity, ya gotta choose between Alpha or her, terrible timing. However, despite being Limited characters, they're both lacking massively. Both were made Attackers, Kuro could've made a new upgraded version of Attacker just like they did with Tanks having Breakers. Which means as soon as an Ice Breaker comes out, Alpha Inverse Crown will be useless and immediately replaced. An absolute middle finger to players and there is the fact that Alpha is probably the most iconic character from PGR yet they did her so dirty, the second most iconic character most likely being Rosetta who at least got a Dark Breaker frame. From what I've experienced, after the DMC Collab was when PGR started devolving and the introduction of Liv Limpidity, or Limited Phylotree Frames, was the big red sign, especially with her being so weak despite her status. Yeah, I am aware that I mostly just complained but like I mentioned, Kuro was always very generous and listened to feedback. Until Wuthering Waves became a thing and they treat it more as their favorite child than PGR. Then they started to delve into typical gacha practices such as abusing FOMO despite being so F2P friendly back in the day. However, there's also the fact that during Alpha Inverse Crown's beta there was definitely player feedback about her being weak and so on, yet Kuro didn't listen to any of the feedback and she didn't change at all. Nonetheless, the music is still good. I lied there, the music during Inverse Crown's patch was bad and sounded very generic. Nowhere near the levels of NARWHAL, LAMIA, and so on; granted its hard to top those, but they still can get good music from Vanguard. The story is nice, but take that opinion with a grain of salt as I stopped doing the story by Chapter 15. Well, at least the gameplay is fun except not anymore; used to be relatively freeform and not so metay, but now its all just meta rotations, technically still can do freeform but don't expect much in the way of success by doing it in competitive modes like PPC or Warzone. Oh yeah, Affixes are a thing; the absolutely worst mechanic ever introduced within PGR with some terrible localization (Ionization/Ion Storm being localized to Plasma Beam or Void being localized as Nihil). I haven't the slightest of how to get started on affixes, but they're different from Elements; they're absolute gimmick mechanics that are not fun because they're so insanely specific at times and absolutely no one liked them yet Kuro still forced it down our throats for whatever reason. Literally have to make specific builds for Affixes that are separate from Elemental builds, different memory sets, and different rotations that are insanely specific at times, alongside different team setups. PPC and Warzone are absolutely filled with metaslaves and whales, if you're neither of those? Good luck with getting any decent rewards or placement. The Babylonia mode had potential, but they completely fumbled it by making it so generic and no real interactivity. Also Kuro really continues to shove the terrible English dub down our throats even if you specifically choose Japanese of Chinese dub. Anyways, that's about all I can think of, truly a wall of text. So overall? I no longer recommend PGR, I lost my love for it, and I might not even come back to it or even want anything to do with it unless Kuro fixes their mistakes, which is something I doubt.

This game is a hidden gem, but not without it's problems. I started playing this game because of the upcoming Kurumi Tokisaki - Date A Live collab. Cons 1. There is one huge problem I believe this game should rework. I it's the very start of the game. Commandant level 1-40, When you are introduced to the game, is probably one of the worst onboarding experiences I've had. I understand it's mostly due to when it was created. The characters used there are severely outdated/boring compared to the endgame/newer. Endgame game-modes are unlocked much later, like 10-20 hours into the game which is typical for gacha games, but I almost thought of giving up the game due to how barebones it felt jumping into the same instances with 2-3 monsters using basic characters. This could prob dissuade off a ton of new players 2. The controls on PC are pretty strange like having L for the ultimate when most things are around WASD. In order for me to fun controls, I had to watch a youtube video of someone 's button bindings and UI organization. Those two really made me re-consider whether it was worth continuing. If not for Kurumi Tokisaki, then I might've just gave it up before I got to the fun part. Pros 1. There's a lot of available endgame content and filler content. But once you've played the game for about 40-60 hours, it levels out, but there's still more filler you can do. 2. The main story is actually pretty interesting, despair, dark and bleak, which I find enjoyable to read. It's also extremely long so there's a lot of content available for those who like going through the entire thing, but I skipped a lot and recapped later. 3. Combat is a tier difficulty higher than most gacha/mobile games and has some nice complexity. It's not impossible to learn, and rotations are eventually optimized. However, the controls/skills have enough depth per character so that if you just press random buttons, nothing much will happen. So you can't just come in as a new player and press random buttons to blast through all the content. Action combat is something I enjoy. 4. Gacha is relatively fair. Supposedly you get enough free rewards to get a character each patch since it's enough to reach pity. Can upgrade characters using other resources as well without having to pull. 5. Skills/animations/character design, skins are very high quality. 6. Also nice soundtrack especially for the vibe they're going for. 7. Additionally, I did visit the PGR booth at Anime Expo, and the team was pretty chill. Even though it's Kuro, it still felt like an indie studio and is still working to deliver for the niche/current playerbase

PRESS Y ON KEYBOARD DURING BATTLE TO FIX CONTOLS _______________________________________________________________ I’ve been playing Punishing: Gray Raven since long before it came to steam and I absolutely love this game. First off, the story is presented as visual novel and starts kinda quiet - world building and setting the scene - but once you hit about chapter 9 it really starts pulling you in. The lore is deep, it’s gritty, and it doesn’t shy away from dark twists. Some chapters get truly heavy, especially around the mid-late game where everything feels hopeless and epic at the same time. It’s not just “fight bad guys” - there are emotional beats, dramatic reveals, and things that actually stick with you as you play through the struggle of humanity against the seemingly undefeatable opponent. The narrative is one of the best I’ve seen in any action RPG that isn’t triple-A console level, and it keeps getting better as you push through. You can play through all of the available story chapters without engaging with gacha system, game gives you demo characters. Now the music might honestly be the secret sauce. The soundtrack is more than background noise - it’s like a trance-fueled adrenaline boost for every fight. From pulsing electronic beats to drum & bass drops that kick in right when you’re slicing through hordes, to ambient tracks that set the mood in story scenes, the audio fits the cyberpunk end-of-the-world aesthetic perfectly. Some tracks hit with explosive trance-leaning electronic beats and soaring synth lines that make every fight feel like it’s scored for a rave-in-space while darker moments are underscored by haunting, atmospheric melodies. Vanguard sound and PGR are a perfect match. Combat is fast, flashy, and stupidly fun - perfect dodges, signature moves, matrix-style slow motion bursts, all synced to pounding beats. They even implemented DMC 5 Vergil and Dante almost with all of their original moves in this game during the collab. Even without newest characters in your roster, you can still clear all of the events/weeklies and earn all the rewards, meta is for competitive players in the leaderboards. And trust me, seeing a perfect rotation of your team’s skills layered over an insane OST hit just hits differently. Speaking of characters - the gacha here is surprisingly kind if you just play regularly. 100% chance of obtaining on the rate up character, all the characters and weapons except for 1 are in standard banners for characters and weapons, you can even select any weapon on the banner and pull for it or just buy it directly in the weapon shop. On the free-to-play front, this game treats players seriously well. If you just play consistently you’ll eventually get every new featured character because income of f2p player is around 15k always which is 1 copy of limited character. That’s pretty rare for this kind of game and makes progression much more chill and satisfying. There are even a few meta-useful characters that are completely free, without temporary time limits, so you don’t feel left behind even as a free-to-play player. Aside from combat and story, there are cool little extras like decorating dorms and building up relationships with your characters, exploring the newest semi open world hub – Babylonia, taking part in guild activities etc.

CACHYOS REVIEW Works out of the box on CachyOS, still has the same jank as Windows if you're running a monitor with a "non-standard" aspect ratio (so anything that's not 4:3 or 16:9) where it doesn't save your resolution whenever you close the game. Just have to manually fullscreen (whichever your DE's equivalent of alt + enter on Windows is) the application once you log in. For the game itself, the story is great once you get past the first 8 chapters. Gameplay can take a bit of getting used to (especially with older characters which still have to worry about orb management) and I would massively recommend actually messing around with UI settings and your keybinds to make it more comfortable to use. Can't really give a detailed comment on the new player experience for "endgame" (LMFAO) since I'm a long time player, but if you're caring about meta as a new player you're gonna be big sad as not only is the invest-gap quite large (not even talking about P2W accounts, but even just older maintained low-invest accounts); but the skill/knowledge-gap is also humongous now. All that said, if you enjoy just reading through VNs and like a bit of action gameplay, it's worth giving a shot. And if you're just wanting to migrate away from W10/11 because of micro$lop, this works just fine on Linux!

Developed and published by KURO GAMES, Punishing: Gray Raven is a free-to-play action RPG that combines high-speed combat with a richly imagined post-apocalyptic science fiction setting. The story unfolds after humanity is nearly driven to extinction by the Punishing Virus, a technological plague that transformed machines into deadly enemies known as the Corrupted. Players assume the role of the Commandant, leading the elite Gray Raven squad of Constructs—advanced cybernetic warriors created to reclaim Earth. While the premise follows familiar themes of survival and resistance, the game distinguishes itself through emotionally driven storytelling, memorable characters, and a world that gradually reveals its history through cinematic missions and character interactions. The narrative balances large-scale conflict with personal moments, encouraging players to become invested in both the fate of humanity and the individuals fighting to restore it. The combat system is undoubtedly the game's defining feature. Battles are built around fluid movement, lightning-fast attacks, and a unique orb-based skill mechanic that rewards timing and strategic planning instead of repetitive button presses. Matching skill orbs to unleash enhanced abilities adds an extra layer of tactical depth, while perfectly timed dodges trigger opportunities for devastating counterattacks. Players can switch between multiple Constructs during combat, allowing them to create stylish combinations and adapt to different enemy types. Every playable character possesses distinct weapons, attack styles, and special abilities, giving each squad composition its own identity. This emphasis on skill-based gameplay keeps encounters exciting throughout the campaign and ensures that mastering mechanics is just as important as strengthening characters. Beyond the battlefield, Punishing: Gray Raven offers several systems that encourage long-term engagement. Character progression involves improving equipment, unlocking new abilities, and collecting additional Constructs to expand tactical options. The game also includes a dormitory feature where players can decorate living spaces and spend time with their squad members. Although this mode is considerably more relaxed than the intense combat sections, it helps strengthen the bond between players and the characters while providing a pleasant change of pace. These quieter activities complement the darker narrative by giving the world a greater sense of personality and reminding players that there is still hope despite the devastation surrounding them. Visually, the game delivers exceptional production quality. Character models are intricately designed, featuring futuristic armor and expressive animations that make every Construct feel unique. Environments range from ruined urban landscapes to advanced technological facilities, all reinforcing the bleak atmosphere of a civilization struggling to survive. Combat effects are colorful and energetic without becoming overwhelmingly chaotic, allowing players to appreciate the spectacular action while maintaining visibility during demanding encounters. The soundtrack further enhances the experience with energetic electronic tracks during battles and emotional orchestral pieces during story sequences, while high-quality voice acting contributes additional weight to important narrative moments. As a free-to-play title, the game naturally includes optional monetization through character acquisition and progression systems. However, its strongest appeal comes from the satisfying gameplay rather than spending money. Players willing to dedicate time to learning the combat mechanics, completing missions, and steadily improving their roster will find a substantial amount of content available without requiring immediate purchases. Frequent updates, new characters, additional story chapters, and challenging endgame activities provide ongoing reasons to return, making the experience feel like a constantly evolving live-service RPG instead of a static release. Punishing: Gray Raven successfully combines stylish action, engaging storytelling, and polished presentation into one of the most impressive free-to-play action RPGs available on PC. Its rewarding combat mechanics, atmospheric world-building, and diverse cast of Constructs create an experience that consistently feels exciting from beginning to end. While the live-service structure and gacha elements may not appeal to every player, they never overshadow the core gameplay, which remains the game's greatest achievement. Fans of fast-paced action games, anime-inspired science fiction, and challenging skill-based combat will find plenty to enjoy, making this a standout title within its genre. Rating: 7/10
